newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Hope replaces dread as Mobutu throws in the towel.
newsitem.headline: Hope replaces dread as Mobutu throws in the towel.

text.p: Zaire's beleaguered capital began the day with newspapers headlining "Panic at the Gates" of the city. By Friday afternoon President Mobutu Sese Seko had abandoned both capital and power, and dread gave way to hope.
Mobutu slipped away in silence. Many speculated he was heading into exile. He refused to the last to give rebel leader Laurent Kabila the satisfaction of an official resignation.
But the people of Kinshasa, a sprawling city of over five million, sensed the tide had finally turned against the man who has ruled them for the past 32 years.
Many prepared to welcome the rebels that Western military sources said were very close to the capital's international airport and only 80 km (50 miles) east of Kinshasa itself.

In a dirt-poor neighbourhood of shanties and slimy puddles, smiling women and children watched painters turn out banners hailing Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL).
"Viva the liberators! Viva the AFDL!" they declared.
Outside the Finance Ministry, some 200 demonstrators displayed their contempt for the crumbling regime's latest bank note, a one-million New Zaire bill bearing Mobutu's portrait.
Incensed by Friday pay-packets they suspect will turn out to be worthless, they stoned official cars, tore up the notes and made gestures indicating the money was no better than toilet-paper.
According to one Kinshasa resident, Mobutu made his way to the airport not in his long, black, official Cadillac but in an expensive Japanese jeep with smoked-glass windows.

"I saw him pass along the (Congo) riverside road just after eight in the morning," the man said. "We know he sometimes uses those cars." Other reports said Mobutu had left at dawn, but there was no independent means of confirming either version.

The government said the president, who is sick with prostate cancer, had gone to his hometown of Gbadolite in northern Zaire. State radio said he would rest there for his health, and kept to their story all day.

One report said the commander of the elite Division Speciale Presidentielle, Mobutu's presidential guard, had left the country. Workers at a private port on the Congo river said General Nzimbi Nzale and his family took a speedboat to the safety of Brazzaville, in the Republic of Congo.
News of Mobutu's exit cheered young opponents who regularly gather at a "street parliament" in Kinshasa.

"If he's gone, we're very, very happy," said Blaise Bomba. "It will mean a new beginning for Zaire. He never did anything for this country. We are ready to welcome Kabila," he added, to cheers from his friends.
While life seemed almost normal on Kinshasa's streets, there was still a rebel army nearing the outskirts and a whiff of anxiety in the air.
As the old power slips away, people fear a vacuum that could trigger a wave of violent looting by Zairean troops, the eternal have-nots of the Mobutu regime, who have nothing left to lose.
